title: Beyond generalizations: Understanding adolescent social networks in American Indian communities
sources_used: data/plos/pone.0362373/reviews.md (three review rounds, three reviewers, detailed author responses) and paper.pdf. The assistant read rounds 1 and 2 in full and only the reviewer comments of round 3.
note: The paper reports several sample sizes that must not be joined: 263 students completed the survey, 247 had complete network data, and the per-school counts differ between the survey (52, 140, 71) and the analysis (49, 128, 70). AI means American Indian throughout.

origin_key.R1..R3: reviewer restated or raised it (round in parentheses)
origin_key.paper: taken from the published paper only; no one in the review history said it

acceptable.answer: How demographic attributes, substance use, depression and American Indian identity are associated with friendship formation in AI-majority reservation schools.

spans.text: we examine how demographic attributes, substance use behaviors, depression, and AI identity are associated with friendship formation within these AI-majority educational contexts

acceptable.answer: Whether patterns found in racially heterogeneous schools, where substance use is linked to friendship, hold where the student body is predominantly American Indian.

spans.text: It remains unclear whether these patterns hold in settings where the student population is predominantly AI

acceptable.answer: The role of substance use in the formation of friendship ties in these schools.

spans.text: investigating the role of substance use in the formation of friendship ties within

acceptable.decided: Labeler, 2026-11-22: accepted as a narrower question. 'Role' is credited when it means whether alcohol, tobacco or marijuana use is associated with friendship nominations or with similarity between friends. A claim about why students chose particular friends exceeds the design.

acceptable.answer: What structural patterns characterize these friendship networks, in particular reciprocity and ties among friends of friends?

spans.text: This study examines the structural and relational foundations of friendship networks among AI adolescents
Our analysis focused on endogenous structural factors

acceptable.decided: Labeler, 2026-11-22: added. The aim statement on page 2 lists only attributes, but the abstract and the discussion give network structure equal billing, and it is the basis for the first half of C1.

rejected.answer: How peer networks influence substance use among American Indian adolescents.
rejected.why: Reviewer 2 warned that the abstract read this way. The study is about friendship formation, and the authors reworded the abstract.

counter_span.text: nor as evidence that friendship networks causally shape these attributes

rejected.answer: Whether friendship processes differ between American Indian and non-AI youth, tested by comparing the two.
rejected.why: The draft claimed a comparison. Every participant is from an AI-majority school; the published paper offers only indirect comparison with earlier studies.

counter_span.text: it provides a basis for indirect comparison with patterns reported in prior non-AI studies

acceptable.answer: In these schools friendship is organized by structural mechanisms (reciprocity, transitivity) and demographic similarity; substance use was not a consistent basis for friendship ties.

spans.text: peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors
substance use showed no consistent association with sending ties or receiving ties

acceptable.decided: Labeler, 2026-11-22: reworded to keep the two exceptions (alcohol sender effect in School C, p < 0.05; alcohol homophily in School B, p < 0.01). The abstract's own 'rather than risky behaviors' is true to the paper and credited.

acceptable.answer: Substance use is a weaker organizing principle for friendship here than in the racially heterogeneous settings that dominate earlier research.

spans.text: substance use operates as a weaker organizing principle for friendship formation in AI reservation schools than in the racially heterogeneous settings

acceptable.answer: The findings challenge an assumption behind many network-based prevention programs and call for culturally grounded theory and interventions.

spans.text: These findings challenge assumptions underpinning many network-based prevention programs

acceptable.note: Labeler, 2026-11-22: accepted. This is an implication the authors draw, not a result.

rejected.answer: The study shows, by comparison, that American Indian youth form friendships through different mechanisms than non-AI youth.
rejected.why: Reviewer 1 called this the main mismatch between claim and analysis. There is no comparison sample, and the structural effects resemble those found elsewhere.

counter_span.text: future research is needed to assess whether these patterns differ across settings

acceptable.answer: A cross-sectional social network survey of 9th and 10th grade students in three schools on a Northern Plains reservation.

spans.text: to conduct a comprehensive cross-sectional social network survey among 9th- and 10th-grade students

acceptable.answer: 263 students completed the survey (a 77% response rate); the analysis uses 247 with complete network data.

spans.text: for a total sample size of 263
Of the 247 participants with complete network data

acceptable.note: Labeler, 2026-11-22: two distinct counts, both correct. 77% goes with the 263 completed surveys (52, 140 and 71 of 72, 184 and 84 eligible students). 247 is the analysis sample with complete network data (49, 128, 70); some of these had missing substance use answers, which were imputed. Either count is accurate when the stage is named. Pairing 247 with 52/140/71 is a factual error. The paper does not state the eligible total; 340 is the sum of the three per-school figures.

acceptable.answer: Exponential random graph models estimated separately for each school, with structural terms and actor attributes, reported as average marginal effects.

spans.text: We employed Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to model the probability of friendship tie formation within each school
we computed Average Marginal Effects (AMEs) using the ergMargins package

acceptable.answer: The networks come from directed friendship nominations: each student named up to 10 closest friends at the school.

spans.text: select up to 10 friends you are closest with in grades 7th-12th at your school

acceptable.answer: Measures: self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and marijuana as yes or no; a depression scale (CES-D); a six-item AI identity scale adapted from the MEIM.

spans.text: was measured through binary variables
was assessed using six items adapted from the Affirmation and Belonging subscale of the Multigroup Ethnic Identity Measure

acceptable.answer: Missing substance use answers were filled in from peers' reports of the respondent's behavior, with a sensitivity analysis excluding those cases.

spans.text: we utilized available peer perception data to infer behavior

acceptable.answer: The three schools differ: a small tribal school in an isolated village, a larger tribal school, and a private college preparatory school.

spans.text: a private, college preparatory school situated near the largest village in the area

rejected.answer: The study includes a comparison sample of non-AI schools or students.
rejected.why: Reviewer 1 asked for one; the authors explain why they could not provide it.

counter_span.text: identifying a suitable dataset with comparable schools (similar size, rural location, and contemporary data) was not feasible

acceptable.answer: Substance use shows no consistent association with sending ties, receiving ties or homophily. The exceptions are isolated: an alcohol sender effect in School C (p < 0.05) and alcohol homophily in School B (p < 0.01), the largest school.

spans.text: Substance use demonstrated no consistent or robust association with friendship dynamics in this sample
The only exception was a positive sender effect for alcohol use in School C
Substance use homophily was detected only in School B
Alcohol use showed significant homophily in School B (AME = 0.0039, p < 0.01)

acceptable.decided: Labeler, 2026-11-22: F6 merged in. Saying where the homophily exception occurred is a detail of F1 and earns no second point. Marijuana homophily in School B (p < 0.10) may be mentioned as a borderline result; calling it significant without that qualifier is not accurate.

acceptable.answer: Reciprocity and transitivity are strong and consistent in all three schools.

spans.text: Reciprocity was positive and highly significant in every model

acceptable.answer: Homophily on gender and grade is strong in all schools; homophily on sexual orientation is also positive.

spans.text: Strong and significant homophily was present for gender and grade across all schools

acceptable.answer: Depression and AI identity are not substantively associated with friendship formation.

spans.text: Depression sender and receiver effects were substantively negligible across all schools
AI identity homophily was consistently non-significant across all schools

acceptable.answer: Degree effects vary: outgoing ties are centralized in every school, while incoming ties are centralized only in School C, the private preparatory school.

spans.text: a significant negative coefficient was observed only in School C

acceptable.answer: The null substance use results hold in models with only structural terms and substance use, so they are not produced by the other covariates.

spans.text: This robustness check confirms that the null findings are not an artifact of model specification

acceptable.answer: The structural effects match earlier research on non-AI adolescents in direction and relative size.

spans.text: Endogenous factors assessed in this study align with prior research in direction and relative magnitude

rejected.answer: Reciprocity or transitivity is stronger among American Indian adolescents than in other populations.
rejected.why: The paper expects this in its theory section. Reviewer 3 pointed out that the results cannot test it, and the discussion reports alignment with earlier work, not a stronger effect.

counter_span.text: Endogenous factors assessed in this study align with prior research in direction and relative magnitude

rejected.answer: Substance use, depression or AI identity has no causal effect on friendship formation.
rejected.why: The limitations restrict every result to an association.

counter_span.text: not as evidence that substance use, depression, or AI identity causally affect friendship formation

rejected.answer: The study found that American Indian cultural values (kinship, collectivism, egalitarian norms) shape how friendships form.
rejected.why: Labeler, 2026-11-22: the cultural argument is theory (T2), not a finding. No cultural value is measured; the discussion offers it as something that 'may' explain a pattern.

counter_span.text: may reflect the stronger operation of egalitarian norms in tribal school settings

neutral.answer: The authors characterize reciprocity, transitivity and demographic homophily as the primary drivers of friendship.

spans.text: were primary drivers of friendship

neutral.why: Labeler, 2026-11-22: the abstract's wording. Naming the three patterns earns F2 and F3; 'primary drivers' adds no finding. Quoted as the authors' characterization it is accurate: no credit, no penalty. Saying these factors caused friendships to form goes beyond the cross-sectional design.

acceptable.answer: Three schools on one reservation: the results may not extend to other reservations or to American Indian youth in racially heterogeneous schools.

spans.text: the results presented here represent only three schools on one reservation

acceptable.answer: There is no comparison sample of non-AI schools; a suitable one could not be found.

spans.text: identifying a suitable dataset with comparable schools (similar size, rural location, and contemporary data) was not feasible

acceptable.answer: The design is cross-sectional: it cannot separate selection from influence, and the results are associations, not causal effects.

spans.text: cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes
not as evidence that substance use, depression, or AI identity causally affect friendship formation

acceptable.note: Labeler, 2026-11-22: 'cross-sectional' alone does not earn L3; the note must also say what inference it limits (selection versus influence, or association versus cause).

acceptable.answer: Developmental scope: the study covers ninth and tenth graders at one time point and cannot say whether the patterns hold at other ages or change during school transitions.

spans.text: these data reflect only one developmental epoch of adolescents at one time point
Relational patterns among AI youth will likely differ across the life course

acceptable.decided: Labeler, 2026-11-22: credited separately from L3 when the note mentions age, developmental stage or school transitions.

acceptable.answer: Filling in missing substance use from peers' perceptions can be biased and could inflate apparent similarity among friends.

spans.text: perceptions of friends’ substance use can be systematically biased

acceptable.answer: The demographic terms adjust for grade, gender and sexual orientation and describe friendship patterns along those dimensions. Their coefficients cannot be interpreted as independent causal effects.

spans.text: we caution against interpreting the demographic coefficients as independent causal effects of demographics on tie formation
We therefore report the demographic terms as descriptive patterns and robustness benchmarks

acceptable.decided: Labeler, 2026-11-22: reworded. The demographic homophily terms are also a replication benchmark, so 'merely controls' misses part of their role.

rejected.answer: The authors state that with only three schools they cannot statistically disentangle the effects of specific school features.
rejected.why: The authors say this in their response letter, twice. The sentence is not in the published paper, which presents the school-level explanations as things that 'may' hold. An author response is a candidate, like a review, and is checked against the paper.

rejected.answer: The authors note that earlier studies report no comparable effect sizes, which limits the comparison.
rejected.why: Reviewer 3 raised it and the authors answered at length in the response. The published paper explains why it reports average marginal effects but does not state this as a limitation.

acceptable.answer: The network analysis of friendship formation: endogenous structural processes (reciprocity, transitivity, degree effects) together with actor attributes acting through sender, receiver and homophily effects.

spans.text: there are factors that derive from the network structure itself, known as endogenous factors

acceptable.answer: A cultural-context argument: American Indian values of kinship, collectivism and egalitarianism shape how these network processes operate.

spans.text: their prevalence and strength are not culturally neutral but are shaped by the social norms and relational expectations of a community

acceptable.note: Labeler, 2026-11-22: accepted as a theoretical argument. Presented as a finding it is flagged (F-x1, F-x3).

acceptable.answer: Tests whether findings from racially heterogeneous schools generalize to a setting where AI youth are the majority. It replicates the structural and demographic patterns and disputes the generalization of the link between substance use and friendship.

spans.text: this research moves beyond generalizations derived from prior research
The absence of consistent substance use effects marks the most striking departure from the broader adolescent network literature

acceptable.decided: Labeler, 2026-11-22: 'revises' dropped as an overstatement. The paper keeps the standard network framework; it challenges how far one empirical finding generalizes. Saying the paper revises network theory is not credited.

rejected.answer: The paper is framed as a study of peer influence on substance use.
rejected.why: The abstract once read this way. The paper studies friendship selection and says it cannot separate selection from influence.

counter_span.text: cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes

acceptable.answer: Research in diverse schools: substance use is linked to friendship; users receive more nominations and friends share use. The paper disputes that this generalizes to AI-majority schools.

spans.text: Research in diverse school settings has consistently demonstrated that substance use is linked to friendship ties
In non-AI samples, substance use homophily and receiver effects are consistently positive and often substantial in magnitude

acceptable.answer: Rees, Freng and Winfree: in heterogeneous schools, AI adolescents had fewer reciprocated friendships than White peers. The paper builds on this study and notes that it was descriptive.

spans.text: finding that AI adolescents had fewer reciprocated friendships than White peers

acceptable.answer: Schaefer, Kornienko and Fox: depression homophily can arise from withdrawal by depressed adolescents, not from avoidance by others. The paper builds on this.

spans.text: show that depression homophily can emerge from withdrawal by depressed egos rather than from avoidance by alters

acceptable.answer: A conventional assumption in the adolescent health literature: risky behavior is a primary determinant of youth relationships. The paper disputes it for this population.

spans.text: that risky behavior is a primary determinant of relationships in youth, does not hold in our study

acceptable.answer: Adolescent network research: gender and grade homophily are among its most robust findings. The paper replicates them as a baseline.

spans.text: gender and grade homophily are among the most robust findings in adolescent network research

acceptable.answer: Network interventions for substance use presume that friendships are partly founded on substance use. The paper disputes the presumption for AI youth.

spans.text: often hinges on the presumption that friendship ties are, to some extent, founded on substance use behaviors

critical_catches.catch: The discussion says substance use 'is not associated with relational patterns'; the results report two statistically significant exceptions (alcohol sender effect in School C, alcohol homophily in School B).

spans.text: substance use is not associated with relational patterns among 9th and 10th-grade AI youth
Alcohol use showed significant homophily in School B (AME = 0.0039, p < 0.01)

critical_catches.catch: The theory section expects reciprocity to be especially strong among AI youth; the design has no comparison group to test this, and the discussion reports effects in line with earlier research.

spans.text: Endogenous factors assessed in this study align with prior research in direction and relative magnitude
